clue.text: Footballer crossing road to get pound

indicators.note: One thing crossing another lies right over it, so the name in front opens up and the road's letters sit inside.

parts.note: Pele is the Brazilian forward a crossword reaches for whenever it wants a footballer
ST is the map shorthand for street, which is a road you can cross

explanation.surface: A footballer running across a road, apparently to collect some money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like the money the surface is chasing, and the sense wanted is the kitchen verb for crushing spices in a mortar.
explanation.definitionFit: To pestle something is to pound it in a mortar, so the tool's name doubles as the verb for the job it does.

clue.text: Coat of plaster like a 2-layer

definitions.note: used as a verb: to layer a plant, pegging a shoot into soil to root

indicators.note: a coat is the outside layer, so only the first and last letters of plaster are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of plaster
2-down is SHEEP, and ovine means sheep-like

explanation.surface: A plasterer describes a coat of plaster as having two layers, like a sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' points to the answer at 2-down, SHEEP. 'Layer' here is the gardening verb, not a stratum.
explanation.definitionFit: To provine is to propagate a vine by layering, bending a branch into the earth so it takes root.

clue.text: What's up with record stock?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: eh is a way of saying what?, and the 's adds an S
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what is going on with a record collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's' becomes EH'S, and 'up' flips it to SHE in this down clue. 'Stock' is livestock, not a shop's goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheep are farm animals, part of a farm's livestock.

clue.text: Pianist leaving church to tour one part of Africa

indicators.note: What leaves has gone, so the two letters named next walk out of the name they were sitting in.
A tour travels right round its subject, so the letters left behind go all the way around the one that follows.

parts.note: Liberace was the candelabra-and-sequins pianist of American television
CE is the Church of England, the usual two letters for church
the Roman numeral for one, a single letter for the tour to close around

explanation.surface: A concert pianist skipping church so as to travel round part of Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pianist leaving church' sounds like a man walking out of a service, and it is an instruction to take two letters out of his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberia is a country on the west African coast, so the definition names it by example: one part of a much bigger continent.

clue.text: Poor shots from Spain's No.1 player in Philadelphia

indicators.note: 'No.1' picks out whatever stands first in the line, and for a word that means the letter it begins with.

parts.note: the letter standing at the front of 'Spain', taken by position rather than looked up
Tom Hanks played the lead in the film Philadelphia

explanation.surface: Spain's top-ranked player mishitting the ball at a tournament in Philadelphia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player in Philadelphia' wants to be a footballer or a tennis seed, and the player meant is the actor who starred in the film of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: A shank is a golf shot struck off the hosel that squirts sideways, the classic bad one, so the plural answers to 'poor shots'.

clue.text: Salesman's wife getting into fish recipe

indicators.note: Getting into something puts you inside it, so the single letter named first ends up within the word named next.

parts.note: hake is the long white sea fish sold at the fishmonger's counter
W is the standing abbreviation for wife
R is recipe, the Latin instruction to take, still written at the head of a prescription

explanation.surface: A salesman's wife joining in with a fish recipe in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is doing two jobs: on the surface it gives the wife an owner, and in the wordplay it is only the join between the definition and everything after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hawker peddles goods from a barrow or door to door, which is a salesman working without a shop behind him.

clue.text: Foolish jester made woollen items for Spooner

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two words exchange their starts

parts.note: a wit is a joker or jester
to knit is to make woollen garments, so knitted; the K is silent

explanation.surface: A court fool who knitted jumpers, as Spooner might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: WIT KNITTED, said aloud, swaps its opening W and N sounds to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitwitted means stupid, like a nitwit or idiot.

clue.text: Performed chore and cried into drink

indicators.note: Tears going into a glass end up inside it, so the crying is placed within the letters of the drink.

parts.note: to sup is to drink, and this is the word that opens up to take something in
wept is the past tense of weeping, which is what crying is

explanation.surface: Somebody who did the housework and then wept into their drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Performed chore' is deliberately vague — it could be a dozen different verbs — and the crossing letters are what tell you which household job is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeping up is the household chore itself, so the past tense of the phrase matches 'performed chore' as a past-tense act.

clue.text: Becks played incredibly to inspire team's midfield for Fergie's old outfit

indicators.note: to inspire is to breathe in, so the middle letters are taken inside the rearranged ones
incredibly suggests something astonishing, so the letters are wildly reordered
the midfield is the centre of the pitch, so the middle letters of the word are used

parts.note: the two middle letters of team

explanation.surface: David Beckham played brilliantly to lift the side's midfield for Alex Ferguson's Manchester United.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants Sir Alex Ferguson and Manchester United; the Fergie meant is the singer. BECKS PLAYED is rearranged ('incredibly') into BLACKEYEDPS, and 'to inspire' breathes in EA, the 'midfield' of team.
explanation.definitionFit: The Black Eyed Peas are the American pop group in which the singer Fergie performed until 2017.

clue.text: Italian dignitary delivers Elon Musk's baby?

definitions.meaning: the title of the elected chief magistrate of the old Venetian republic
the cost-cutting department he set up in Washington, and the meme coin he kept posting about

explanation.surface: An Italian bigwig handing over Elon Musk's newborn child.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags how loose the second half is: 'baby' means a pet project rather than a child, and the two senses are centuries apart.
explanation.definitionFit: A doge headed the republics of Venice and Genoa, and the same four letters are the acronym of Musk's Department of Government Efficiency.

clue.text: Ring with number for trendsetter

parts.note: a bell is the thing that rings, the noun sitting behind the verb
W is the standard shorthand for 'with', as written on a menu or a recipe card
read as one that numbs: ether was the anaesthetic surgeons dosed patients with

explanation.surface: An instruction to telephone somebody on a particular number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is the trap. It is not a figure at all but a thing that makes you numb, which is how what looks like a comparative adjective turns into an anaesthetic.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellwether is the lead sheep wearing the bell that the flock follows, so it names anything the rest take their cue from.

clue.text: Duck followed by a bird

indicators.note: What follows comes along behind, so the letters named second are written after the letters named first.

parts.note: to duck out of the way is to dip
'per' means 'a' in phrases like sixty miles an hour

explanation.surface: A duck paddling along with another bird behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the bird and turns out to be the verb, and the little word 'a' is material rather than grammar: twice a day is twice per day.
explanation.definitionFit: The dipper is the river bird that walks under water to feed, so 'bird' is the plain category the name belongs to.

clue.text: Pervert chose ITV2

indicators.note: To pervert a thing is to twist it out of its proper form, and letters twisted like that come out in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Somebody settling down in front of ITV2 for the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: The channel name is split down the middle: the three letters belong to the wordplay and the digit beside them is a cross-reference to 2 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheviots are the hardy hill sheep bred along the Scottish border, so the plural answers to what 2 down names.

clue.text: Comic Stewart Lee forgetting line 2

indicators.note: comic as an adjective means funny or absurd, so the letters are jumbled
forgetting means the line letter is left out

explanation.surface: The comedian Stewart Lee forgets his lines in the second act.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' points to 2-down, SHEEP. Stewart Lee is a British stand-up comedian; 'forgetting line' takes L out, leaving STEWARTEE, which 'Comic' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Teeswater is a breed of longwool sheep from Teesdale in northern England.

clue.text: Fencing covers problem for 2 poets

parts.note: sheep scab is the mite disease that plagues a flock, the problem the cross-reference points at
a bard is a poet, Shakespeare being the Bard

explanation.surface: A fence hiding some trouble that a pair of poets have got into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fencing' reads as the wire round a field, which is where the surface wants you; the sport is meant instead, and 'covers' is a noun rather than a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Scabbards are the sheaths a sword slides into, so they are the covers that belong to fencing blades.

clue.text: Backing favourites to show pace

indicators.note: Backing a thing turns it round to face the other way, and in an across answer that means the letters read right to left.

parts.note: a favourite is a pet: a teacher's pet, a pet project

explanation.surface: Punters putting their money on the favourites to run quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing favourites' is one phrase at the bookmaker's, and the split falls inside it: the first word is the instruction and the second is the material.
explanation.definitionFit: A step and a pace are the same unit of walking, one movement of one foot, so either word measures out a distance.

clue.text: 'Dog in the mirror' is entertaining answer for god

indicators.note: A mirror shows everything the other way round, so the dog's letters go in back to front.
To entertain somebody is to have them inside your house, so these letters hold another one within them.

parts.note: a lab is a labrador, the retriever kept as a family dog
A is the standard abbreviation for answer, as in a Q and A session

explanation.surface: A dog amusing itself with its own reflection.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Dog in the mirror' look like the title of a photograph, and they are the setter's way of parcelling up an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Baal was the Canaanite storm god denounced all through the Old Testament, so 'god' names him about as plainly as it can.

clue.text: Unfinished Monster Munches regularly account for fires

indicators.note: munching means eating, so the shortened monster takes the other letters inside
unfinished means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a beast is a monster

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of account

explanation.surface: Monster Munch, a British corn snack, is half-eaten while someone explains the fires.
explanation.walkthrough: Monster Munch is a British snack brand, which makes 'Monster' look like part of a name. The alternate letters of account here are CON.
explanation.definitionFit: Beacons are signal fires lit on hilltops to send warnings.

clue.text: Ambassador's wife getting tips from Ascension Islander

parts.note: HE is His Excellency, the formal style of address for an ambassador
a bride is a wife on her wedding day

indicators.note: The tips of a word are the points at either end of it, so its first and last letters are what come away.

parts.note: the letters standing at the two tips of 'Ascension'

explanation.surface: An ambassador's wife picking up tips from somebody who lives on Ascension Island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ascension Islander' reads as one person from that South Atlantic rock, and the definition is only its second word — the island group meant is off the coast of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hebridean is somebody from the Hebrides, so the answer names an islander by the particular islands they come from.

clue.text: Male chimney sweep in dance company

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep
Bert is the sweep Dick Van Dyke plays in Mary Poppins

explanation.surface: A man who sweeps chimneys taking his place in a dance troupe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Male' is the whole of the wordplay's first half rather than an adjective attached to the sweep, which is what keeps the two of them looking like one man.
explanation.definitionFit: Rambert, founded by Marie Rambert, is Britain's oldest dance company, so the definition names the institution by what it is.

clue.text: Spider has distinctive pattern on behind occasionally

indicators.note: In a down clue whatever is 'on' something sits above it, so the pattern's letters are entered first, at the top of the column.

parts.note: Aran is the cabled knitting pattern named after the islands off Galway

indicators.note: Occasional letters are the ones taken now and then rather than all of them, here every second letter of the word.

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of 'behind'

explanation.surface: A spider carrying unusual markings on its rear end.
explanation.walkthrough: The knitting is the piece most solvers miss: Aran jumpers are the heavy cream ones covered in raised cables, and the word is a pattern before it is anything else.
explanation.definitionFit: An araneid is any member of Araneae, the spider order, so the definition is the everyday word for the zoologist's one.

clue.text: Stuck-up date tucking into revolutionary food

indicators.note: the turned date goes inside the revolutionary's name

parts.note: Che Guevara is the archetypal crossword revolutionary

indicators.note: in a down clue, stuck-up means the word is set upwards, read backwards

parts.note: to see someone is to date them

explanation.surface: A snooty dinner companion gets stuck into a revolutionary's meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck-up' looks like a snobbish description; in this down clue it turns SEE into EES.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheese is a food made from milk curds.

clue.text: Dear Charlie Dance showing a bit of flesh

parts.note: a lamb is a term of endearment: 'the poor lamb' means the poor dear
Charlie is C in the radio alphabet
a hop is a dance, as in a village hop

explanation.surface: The actor Charles Dance turning up in a revealing scene.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make 'Charlie Dance' look like Charles Dance, the British actor, and both words are ordinary vocabulary doing quite separate jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamb chop is a cut of meat off the ribs, so 'a bit of flesh' describes it as one piece of an animal.

clue.text: Untidy Womble briefly embracing a form of anarchy

indicators.note: An untidy room has everything in the wrong place, and untidy letters are out of their proper order too.
An embrace gathers something in, so the letter named next joins the pile being shuffled.
Said briefly, a word is cut short, so the name gives up its final letter.

parts.note: the Wombles are the litter-collecting creatures of a British children's series, and this one arrives a letter short
the bare article, taken in as one more letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: A scruffy Womble clinging on while everything descends into anarchy.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that Wombles are famously tidy, forever clearing up other people's litter, so 'untidy' looks like a description of the creature rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Mob law is what obtains when a crowd enforces its own will instead of the courts, so it is one particular form anarchy takes.

clue.text: Club accepting the French complaint

indicators.note: Accepting something is taking it in, so the club's letters open up to hold the two that follow.

parts.note: a bat is a club you swing
'le' is French for 'the', a standard two-letter import

explanation.surface: A club taking on a grievance raised in French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' is crossword shorthand for the French word for 'the', which is LE or LA depending on which the letters want.
explanation.definitionFit: A bleat is a whining complaint, the noun borrowed from the sheep's cry and used for any feeble grumble.

clue.text: 2 drunk cider or beer

indicators.note: A drunk cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state will not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
beer is ale, and the synonym joins the fodder rather than the word itself

explanation.surface: Somebody who has had far too much cider or beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beer' is not fodder as it stands: it has to be turned into its three-letter synonym before the letters will come out right.
explanation.definitionFit: The Corriedale is a New Zealand crossbred kept for wool and meat, so it is one of the animals 2 down names.

clue.text: Females take drugs orally

indicators.note: What is done orally is done by mouth, so the wordplay hands you a sound and leaves the spelling to you.

parts.note: to use is to take drugs, and said aloud that word is written down quite differently

explanation.surface: Women being told to take their medicine by mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take drugs orally' reads as an instruction off a pill packet, and 'orally' carries none of that sense: it is the flag that a sound is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewes are the female sheep of a flock, so 'Females' names them by sex, the plural matching the plural.

clue.text: South American relations in part of England

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
US does duty for American, the adjective taken from the country's initials
relations in this sense is the polite word for it

explanation.surface: A South American's family connections somewhere in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South American' looks like one nationality and is two separate pieces, which is what keeps the next word looking like cousins and aunts.
explanation.definitionFit: Sussex is the county along the south coast below London, so the definition names it by example, one county out of forty-odd.

clue.text: Declared dead by the entrance of Serpentine Gallery

indicators.note: An entrance is the way in at the front, so what is taken is the letter standing at the front of the word.

parts.note: the letter at the front of 'Serpentine'
Tate is the gallery a crossword means when it says gallery
D is the standard abbreviation for dead

explanation.surface: A death being announced at the door of the Serpentine Gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Serpentine Gallery, in London's Kensington Gardens, is a real place, so the two words hold together on the surface while the wordplay cuts between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To state something is to declare it, and the past tense of the one stands in for the past tense of the other.
